notable_claims: MIT's speech code defines harassment broadly enough to include conduct that creates an 'offensive educational, work, or living environment'.
The MIT guide suggests consequences for violating the code can include termination of employment or student status.
Campus speech codes are viewed by the author as a tool for administrators to increase their power over students and faculty.
classification.summary: Bob Chatelle criticizes a new speech code at MIT titled "Dealing With Harassment at MIT," arguing that its broad definition of harassment creates a mechanism for censorship. He contends that treating free speech as an 'interest' rather than an inalienable right allows administrators to suppress offensive speech under the guise of maintaining a non-hostile environment. Chatelle warns that such codes ultimately empower authorities and disproportionately harm minority students.
classification.title: "Democracy is Not For the Thin Skinned" (on the MIT speech code)

identity.subject: [NWU] "Democracy is Not For the Thin Skinned" (on the MIT speech code)

notable_claims: The term 'lascivious' in child pornography law is subjective and lacks objective meaning.
Government sting operations like Operation Looking Glass targeted citizens by inducing them to buy materials that were legal where produced.
Child pornography laws can be used to criminalize non-obscene art and literature, such as the works of Robert Mapplethorpe.
organizations: Supreme Court of the United States
classification.summary: An excerpt from the National Writers Union's Political Issues Committee newsletter discussing the 'moral panic' surrounding child pornography laws. The author argues that subjective legal terms like 'lascivious' allow for government overreach and censorship of art, photography, and literature. It highlights the risks of state-sponsored sting operations and the potential for these laws to be used against law-abiding citizens.
classification.title: Kiddie Porn Panic

notable_claims: The University of Waterloo banned a specific newsgroup.
classification.summary: Stephen Urquhart reports that the University of Waterloo has banned a specific newsgroup. This instance highlights early institutional censorship of Usenet communication within academic environments.
classification.title: Waterloo University bans this newsgroup

notable_claims: The university suspended a specific newsgroup to comply with a court order issued by Justice Francis Kovacs.
classification.summary: McMaster University administration ordered the removal of materials regarding the Karla Teale trial from university computer systems. This action included the suspension of the alt.fan.karla-homolka newsgroup to avoid potential charges of contempt of court.
classification.title: Karla Teale Trial Court Order

notable_claims: The University of Waterloo administration ordered the removal of content from its network to comply with a judicial publication ban.
classification.summary: University of Waterloo Provost Jim Kalbfleisch directed the university librarian and associate provost (computing) to remove materials violating a court-ordered publication ban. The directive specifically targeted both physical newspapers in the library and information distributed via an Internet newsgroup to avoid charges of contempt of court.
classification.title: Tuesday, December 1

notable_claims: The McGill EE department formally recognized personal computer files and email as private via a motion passed with no votes against on December 2, 1993.
classification.summary: The Department of Electrical Engineering at McGill University passed a motion declaring that personal files, electronic mail, and other electronic communications are to be considered private. The move was prompted by an increase in electronic correspondence and student concerns regarding privacy in the electronic workplace.
classification.title: McGill U. EE department recognizes computer privacy

identity.subject: McGill U. EE department recognizes computer privacy

notable_claims: The university administration suspended account access to stop 'subversive activity' involving controversial newsgroup posts.
Administrators claimed that using university machines for 'controversial agendas' reflected badly on the institution.
University administrations were perceived as self-censoring due to fear of public or legal reprisal.
classification.summary: Adam Glover discusses the suspension of his computer account at the University of Toronto's Engineering Computer Facility (ECF) after posting a Washington Post article to mainstream newsgroups. The administration justified the action by stating they would not tolerate 'controversial' agendas on their machines, citing concerns over hate propaganda. Glover argues that university administrations were being scared into self-censorship due to fear of reprisal and political pressure.
classification.title: Re: Public Letter to Warren Jackson (was Re: selective newsfeed drops)
